messages.text: What is non-signaling tester, and which product-related measurement decisions depend on understanding it?

The knowledge base did **not validate a complete answer**; it found partial evidence but reported the direct relationship as insufficient. So treat this as a grounded summary plus clearly limited interpretation.

A **non-signaling tester** is an RF tester used when the device under test is measured **without establishing a live protocol/signaling connection** such as a cellular call, network registration, or Wi‑Fi association. Instead, the DUT is put into a test/production mode and RF transmit/receive measurements are made directly. The knowledge result specifically notes that, in a WLAN production context, RF measurements are performed in **non-signaling mode to save time**, and identifies the **R&S CMP180 Radio Communication Tester** as the related Rohde & Schwarz product example. It contrasts this with the **R&S CMX500 5G one-box signaling tester**, which is positioned for signaling/R&D-style testing. Evidence cited by the knowledge result includes Raw files for CMX500 and CMP180 product identity: `raw/Productions/PR/CMX500 AI Scripting Assistant...md` and `raw/Productions/CMP180_specs_en_3609-7348-22_v0800.md`.

Product-related measurement decisions that depend on understanding “non-signaling” include:

| Decision | Why non-signaling matters | R&S example |
|---|---|---|
| **Signaling vs non-signaling instrument choice** | If you need realistic connection behavior, use a signaling tester; if you need fast production RF measurements, use non-signaling. | **CMX500** for signaling; **CMP180** for non-signaling production RF. |
| **R&D vs production test strategy** | R&D often needs network/AP emulation and protocol behavior; production usually prioritizes speed, repeatability, and throughput. | CMX500 for R&D signaling; CMP180 for manufacturing RF test. |
| **WLAN option selection** | Non-signaling WLAN production testing requires options for specific standards and modes, e.g. 802.11ax/be SISO or MIMO. | CMP180 WLAN options such as 802.11ax, 802.11be, MIMO, PER-related measurements were listed in the knowledge result, though not fully validated as Raw-grounded. |
| **Frequency range decision** | You must know whether the non-signaling tester covers the device’s bands, e.g. 6 GHz or 8 GHz operation. | CMP180 with extended frequency range option was mentioned. |
| **Bandwidth decision** | Wi‑Fi 7/advanced WLAN production tests may require wide bandwidth support. | CMP180 500 MHz bandwidth option was mentioned. |
| **MIMO architecture decision** | Non-signaling production test setups may need enough analyzers/generators/RF ports for 2x2, 4x4, or higher MIMO. | CMP180 architecture/scaling for MIMO was mentioned. |
| **Throughput/cost-of-test decision** | Non-signaling mode is typically chosen because it reduces test time versus full signaling connection setup. | CMP180 production use case. |
| **Cellular vs Wi‑Fi coverage decision** | A product team must decide whether the tester needs to cover cellular, WLAN, Bluetooth, or mixed connectivity in non-signaling mode. | CMP180 was identified as covering production RF roles; details need confirmation from product specs. |

In short: understanding “non-signaling” determines whether you choose a **fast RF production tester like CMP180** or a **protocol/signaling tester like CMX500**, and it drives the required options for standard coverage, frequency range, bandwidth, MIMO, and production throughput.

data.answer:
已查到可引用的部分資料：

A non-signaling tester is an RF measurement tester used when the DUT is measured in non-signaling mode rather than in a signaling connection; in the WLAN production context, the passages state that all RF measurements are performed in non-signaling mode to save time [2].
R&S CMP180 is the Rohde & Schwarz product example positioned for this non-signaling production RF role, and the supplied RAW evidence identifies it as the “Rohde & Schwarz CMP180 Radio Communication Tester” [2][67].
R&S CMX500 is the contrasting signaling example for R&D, and the supplied RAW evidence identifies it as the “CMX500 5G one-box signaling tester” [1][65].
| Product-related measurement decision | What depends on understanding “non-signaling” | Rohde & Schwarz example | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| R&D signaling vs production non-signaling instrument choice | Use CMX500 when the task is signaling-mode R&D RF TX/RX testing under real-world conditions, and use CMP180 when the task is production RF measurement in non-signaling mode [1][2]. | R&S CMX500 for R&D signaling, R&S CMP180 for production non-signaling RF measurements [1][2]. | RAW supports CMX500 as a one-box signaling tester and CMP180 as a Radio Communication Tester [65][67]. |
| WLAN standard measurement option choice | CMP180 WLAN measurement choices include 802.11a/b/g/n/ac SISO, 802.11ax SISO, 802.11be SISO, WLAN true MIMO 2x2/4x4, WLAN true MIMO 5x5/6x6, and WLAN packet error rate acknowledgement measurements [40]. | R&S CMP-KM350, R&S CMP-KM351, R&S CMP-KM352, R&S CMP-KM360, R&S CMP-KM361, and R&S CMP-KM365 [40]. | RAW supports the CMP180 product identity, while the option details are supported by the WIKI specifications summary [67][40]. |
| Cellular vs non-cellular production measurement coverage | CMP180 supports many cellular and non-cellular technologies, including Wi-Fi 6E, Wi-Fi 7, and 5G NR FR1 up to 8 GHz with bandwidths up to 500 MHz [2]. | R&S CMP180 non-signaling RF tester [2]. | RAW supports CMP180 as a Rohde & Schwarz Radio Communication Tester [67]. |
| Frequency extension decision | CMP180 ordering information lists R&S CMP-K168 as the extended frequency range option from 6 GHz to 8 GHz [34]. | R&S CMP-K168 [34]. | RAW supports the CMP180 product identity, while the frequency-extension option is supported by WIKI [67][34]. |
| Bandwidth decision | CMP180 ordering information lists R&S CMP-K185 as the 500 MHz bandwidth option [34]. | R&S CMP-K185 [34]. | RAW supports the CMP180 product identity, while the bandwidth option is supported by WIKI [67][34]. |
| MIMO production architecture decision | CMP180 integrates two analyzers, two generators and two sets of eight RF ports, so one box supports 2x2 MIMO testing [2]. | One R&S CMP180 for 2x2 MIMO testing [2]. | RAW supports CMP180 as the product, while the MIMO architecture claim is supported by WIKI [67][2]. |
| 4x4 MIMO scaling decision | Two CMP180 instruments can be combined and scaled to support four analyzers and generators for efficient testing of 4x4 MIMO access points [2]. | Two R&S CMP180 instruments for 4x4 MIMO access point testing [2]. | RAW supports CMP180 as the product, while the 4x4 scaling claim is supported by WIKI [67][2]. |
| Future-waveform evaluation decision | CMP180 was described as demonstrating loopback validation of a 480 MHz WLAN waveform, described as a potential candidate for yet-to-be-defined Wi-Fi 8 / IEEE 802.11bn rather than a formal Wi-Fi 8 specification [2]. | R&S CMP180 loopback mode demonstration [2]. | RAW supports CMP180 as the product, while the 480 MHz loopback claim is supported by WIKI [67][2]. |
| Signaling Wi-Fi configuration decision | CMX500 WLAN signaling options include 802.11a/b/g/n/ac, 802.11ax, 802.11be, 802.11bn, AP testing, station testing, 2x2 MIMO, and advanced encryption and authentication [18]. | R&S CMX-KS350B, R&S CMX-KS351B, R&S CMX-KS352B, R&S CMX-KS353B, R&S CMX-KS355B, R&S CMX-KS356B, R&S CMX-KS357B, R&S CMX-KS360B, and R&S CMX-KS365B [18]. | RAW supports CMX500 as a one-box signaling tester, while the signaling option list is supported by WIKI [65][18]. |
